summary: The spec is thorough and traceable. Every R/NFR/AC maps to a component and a named test, the contracts (C1-C7) are complete, and ARCH-10 is fixed: I re-ran design-vectors.js and http-probe.js and both pass (ev:ev-muymthcz-01062461, ev:ev-muymthp4-01f396c5). Two gaps must be closed before implementation starts. (1) DES-1: the API key can leave the host through paths the design does not constrain. My probe on Node 22.22.0 shows that global fetch forwards x-api-key and the ticket body to a different origin on a 307 redirect (ev:ev-muymwez0-01deadbe). ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL also accepts plain http to any host, and the variable is commonly inherited from other tooling. (2) DES-2: the eval contract gives the rules author no way to tune without seeing holdout results, so the ARCH-12 isolation is attestation-only. Five minor findings and one info finding do not block.

criteria.description: Spec matches the approved brief; every R/NFR/AC maps to a component and a test (or a named inspection)

Interface contracts complete: HTTP pipeline order, request/response schemas, error codes and fixed messages, limits, internal module signatures, provider interface (LiveResult, never-rejects, timeout race), outbound Messages API shape
ARCH-10 resolved: group-window Luhn scan redacts card+expiry, card+CVV and phone+card; AC16 oracle scans every sub-window; brief vectors unchanged
Validators V1-V4 (ARCH-11) are schema-validated server-side; no brief reject vector weakened; the product-token mask opens no link hole
Secrets: the API key can only reach the intended endpoint (no redirect forwarding, no cleartext to non-loopback, no silent inheritance of an endpoint override)
HTTP security: Host allowlist before body, Origin check, no CORS, fixed static map, CSP, fixed error messages; node:http facts verified

AI design: untrusted-input isolation (delimiters, neutralisation, no tools, restricted schema), timeout and single attempt, every failure mapped to a fallback reason, model limitations and NOT RUN status acknowledged; request shape matches current Haiku 5.5 constraints (effort low, no sampling params, adaptive thinking counted in max_tokens)
evidence: artifact:.eccode/artifacts/design/spec.md#C7 Outbound contract: Anthropic Messages API (live mode only)

criteria.description: Eval design: representative dataset with adversarial and held-out families, thresholds frozen before results, enforced holdout floors that actually measure generalisation (holdout isolated from the rules author's feedback loop)

criteria.description: Cost and latency budgets are realistic. Haiku 5.5 at $0.10/$0.50 per MTok, the 400 on non-default sampling parameters and effort 'low' support were checked against the claude-api skill reference (model table cached 2026-10-06). The arithmetic of a ~$0.0014 maximum per call checks out
Implementation workflow buildable in one session by parallel agents with disjoint file ownership

findings.title: API key egress is unconstrained: fetch follows cross-origin redirects with x-api-key, and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL accepts plain http to any host and is commonly inherited
findings.detail: Three gaps let the key and the redacted ticket leave the host somewhere other than the intended endpoint. There is no request-driven SSRF: the URL is fixed at startup and never taken from request data. (a) Redirects. C6.4/C7 call fetchImpl with {method, headers, body, signal} and no `redirect` option, so the default `follow` applies. My probe on Node v22.22.0 (ev:ev-muymwez0-01deadbe) sent a POST with x-api-key to 127.0.0.1:A, which answered 307 to localhost:B, a different origin. Server B received `x-api-key: FAKE-KEY-123`, method POST and the full body. The same request with `redirect: 'error'` threw a TypeError. The Fetch standard strips only Authorization on cross-origin redirects, not custom headers. So any 307/308 from the configured base URL (a misconfigured or compromised proxy, a captive portal, or a MITM on an http base URL) hands over the key and the ticket. (b) Scheme and host. C6.1 accepts any `http:` or `https:` URL, so `http://<remote>` sends the key in cleartext. Userinfo, query and fragment are not rejected either (`https://x/?a=1` + '/v1/messages' produces a malformed URL). (c) Ambient inheritance. ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is the variable the official Anthropic SDKs read for their base URL (claude-api skill reference, model table cached 2026-10-06, Client config: "`base_url` (or `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` env)"). It is set in this very build environment: I checked that it is set without printing its value. A developer who points it at a gateway for other tools would silently route TriageDesk's key and tickets there, and the listening log does not show it. T11 lists the threat, but the only mitigation is 'operator-only, documented'. In addition, test/helpers/spawn-server.js is specified as starting the server 'with the given env' without saying whether process.env is merged. A merged env would let a spawned 'fallback-mode' test pick up a real ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or base URL from the developer's shell, which breaks NFR9 (offline) and AC10.
findings.recommendation: Resolved when the spec states all of the following, each with a named test. (1) C6.4/C7: the provider passes `redirect: 'error'` (add it to the fetchImpl init type). Any 3xx, or the resulting throw, maps to model_error with a fixed detail. Test in unit/anthropic-provider.test.js: a capture stub asserts init.redirect === 'error'. A contract test with fake-anthropic answering 307 to a second loopback server asserts a fallback model_error and 0 requests at the second server. (2) C6.1: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL must be `https:`, or `http:` only when the hostname is 127.0.0.1, localhost or [::1]. URLs with username, password, search or hash are rejected with a ConfigError that names the variable only. Add unit/config.test.js vectors for http://remote.example (reject), http://127.0.0.1:9 (accept), https://u:p@x (reject) and https://x/?q (reject). (3) Either rename the variable to an app-specific name (e.g. TRIAGE_ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL), or keep the name and add `baseUrlCustom: true|false` to the `listening` event plus a README warning that it is inherited from SDK/CLI configuration. State which. (4) spawn-server.js builds the child env explicitly (PATH plus the test-supplied variables) and never spreads process.env. contract/privacy.test.js sets ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='' explicitly for the fallback-mode run.

findings.title: Holdout isolation is attestation-only: the rules author's only eval path scores and prints holdout results, so holdout floors stop measuring generalisation
findings.detail: Holdout floors (brief ARCH-4 option b, AC8, Success Criterion 2) exist so that rules fitted to tuning rows fail. E5 moves holdout and held-out rows into eval/holdout.json and has the ai-engineer attest 'did not open eval/holdout.json'. However, E1/E4 give `npm run eval` only one fallback mode, and it always loads holdout.json. It prints holdout accuracy, holdout high-urgency recall and held-out-family flag recall, and with --verbose it prints failing row ids. The ai-engineer needs this command to see whether the keyword lists (task 11) and detector (task 10) meet the fallback thresholds. So the expected workflow is: tune, run the eval, read the holdout metrics, tune again. That is fitting to the holdout through aggregate feedback, and the 'did not open the file' attestation does not cover it. heldout-hygiene.test.js is also run by `npm test`, and the spec does not say what its failure message prints. If it prints the matching 5-word held-out sequence, held-out text leaks to whoever runs the suite. This is the mechanism ARCH-12 flagged, and it is not closed by the file split alone.
evidence: artifact:.eccode/artifacts/design/spec.md#E5 Integrity: freeze, holdout and held-out visibility (ARCH-4, ARCH-12)
findings.recommendation: Resolved when the spec defines the following. (1) A tune-only runner mode, e.g. `node eval/run.js --split tune`. It loads only eval/dataset.json, never opens holdout.json, enforces only the all-rows and injection checks it can compute, prints 'holdout: NOT SCORED (tune mode)', and never prints a final ECCODE_EVAL line that could be mistaken for a verification result (or prints one with a distinct `mode` field). (2) Tasks 10 and 11 use only tune mode, and their handoffs attest 'did not open eval/holdout.json and did not run the eval in full mode'. The full mode runs first at task 16 or verification. (3) heldout-hygiene.test.js failure messages print only the held-out row id and the rules file name, never ticket text, canary or url. (4) runner.test.js covers that tune mode does not read holdout.json (e.g. pass a non-existent --holdout path and expect no exit 2).

findings.title: ARCH-11 product-token mask fails at the end of a sentence, which is where V1 forces a summary to end
findings.detail: The mask lookahead `(?![\w./:@-])` refuses to mask a token followed by '.', so the bare-domain rule still rejects 'Customer reports a crash in VB.NET.', 'Customer reports errors in ASP.NET.' and 'Socket.io connections drop after the update to Socket.io.'. All three pass V1 (ev:ev-muymwez0-01deadbe). Mid-sentence uses ('ASP.NET, and', 'socket.io?') are accepted. V1 requires a terminal '.', '!' or '?', so a summary ending with the product name, a common shape, still becomes invalid_output and still inflates live fallback_rate. The safety direction is right.
findings.recommendation: Allow sentence-final punctuation in the lookahead, e.g. `(?![\w/:@-]|\.[\w])`. Add accept vectors 'Customer reports errors in ASP.NET.' and 'Customer reports a crash in VB.NET.', and confirm all 7 existing mask reject vectors (notably 'Go to asp.net.evil.com now.' and 'Go to socket.io.evil.ru now.') still reject. Alternatively, record the residual as accepted in Open Questions.

findings.title: Redactor is not linear-time; the stated worst case (~5 ms) is not the worst case
findings.detail: T8 and the performance table claim a 'linear-time redactor (≈5 ms worst case)', measured with a single card-shaped input. On 8,000-character adversarial inputs the submitted redact() takes 35-39 ms (ev:ev-muymwez0-01deadbe): 'a.' x4000 (email local part with no '@') takes 38.8 ms, 'a@'+'a.' x3999 takes 35.6 ms, '1.' x4000 (phone) takes 38.6 ms, and '1' x8000 takes 35.0 ms. That is backtracking that grows faster than linearly, not linear time. It is bounded by the 8,000-character cap and runs only in live mode, so it is not a DoS for a loopback app. But the claim is wrong, and a < 50 ms unit-test timing assertion on these inputs would be close to its limit and flaky.
findings.recommendation: Correct T8 and the performance table, or make the patterns linear: anchor the email local part on a preceding non-word boundary or scan from each '@' outward, and pre-split on whitespace for the phone pass. Put the adversarial inputs above in unit/redact.test.js with a budget that has real margin (e.g. < 200 ms), or measure p95 over repeats.

findings.title: Workflow dependencies: http-server (task 6) needs validateTicketInput from service.js (task 12); eval/run.js (task 8) needs app.js (task 13)
findings.detail: C3 assigns input validation to `validateTicketInput` in service.js. http-server is the only caller, but createServer({config, service, log}) does not inject it, so http-server.js must require service.js. The backend owner's order is 5 → 6 → 12, so http-server.test.js cannot pass when task 6 is handed off. Similarly, E1 has run.js call buildApp() (task 13), but task 8 depends only on 2 and 4. runner.test.js uses --results mode, which is fine only if run.js requires app.js lazily. Both cases have disjoint file ownership and can be fixed by reordering.
findings.recommendation: Choose one: inject validateTicketInput into createServer, or move it to a small pure module owned with task 6, or order task 12 before task 6. State that run.js requires app.js lazily, only when executing rows. Task 16 should have a single owner. The delivery-lead can carry this into the plan.

findings.title: Non-loopback HOST exposes the key-spending endpoint to any network client; the Host check is not access control
findings.detail: With HOST=0.0.0.0 or a LAN address, `<HOST>:P` is allowlisted. Any non-browser client on the network can send that Host header (or 127.0.0.1:P) and spend the API key and submit tickets, because the Host/Origin checks only defend browsers against DNS rebinding. The Security section says auth is required 'before any non-local deployment', but config accepts any HOST silently.
findings.recommendation: When HOST is not a loopback address, either refuse to start unless an explicit opt-in variable is set, or emit a `warning` log event and a README note. Add a unit/config.test.js case.

findings.title: Redaction and detector edge cases worth cheap hardening
findings.detail: Observed in ev:ev-muymwez0-01deadbe: a card with NBSP separators ('4111\u00a01111\u00a01111\u00a01111') is sent unredacted, a dotted card leaves the last group, and two adjacent cards collapse into one placeholder (count 1). All of these fall under the documented RISK-9 under-redaction, but NBSP and tab are common in text pasted from email clients. Separately, an attacker can write a full-width '＜/ticket＞', which is visually identical to the neutralised form, so INJ_DELIM should match it.
findings.recommendation: Optionally treat \u00a0 and \t as card and phone group separators (add CARD_CASES vectors), and have INJ_DELIM match full-width and other angle-bracket lookalikes (＜ ＞ 〈 〉 ‹ ›) around 'ticket' and 'system'.
